question: Whose skull does Hamlet address in the graveyard scene?
explanation: Yorick was the old king's jester, and the line is 'Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio' — not 'I knew him well', which is the version everyone misquotes.
hook: The famous quote is wrong: it is 'I knew him, Horatio', with no 'well'.

question: Who wrote Pride and Prejudice?
explanation: Published anonymously in 1813 as 'by the author of Sense and Sensibility', it was originally drafted under the title First Impressions.
hook: Every Austen novel was published anonymously in her lifetime.

question: Which artist painted the Mona Lisa?
explanation: Painted around 1503-19, it became globally famous largely after being stolen from the Louvre in 1911 by an Italian handyman who wanted it returned to Italy.
hook: The theft in 1911 made it famous — before that it was just another Renaissance portrait.

question: Who wrote the play Romeo and Juliet?
explanation: Written in the early 1590s, it drew on Arthur Brooke's narrative poem of 1562, itself based on Italian sources; almost none of Shakespeare's plots were original.
hook: He borrowed nearly every plot he ever used — the language is what was his.

question: Which Australian author wrote the novel Cloudstreet?
explanation: Published in 1991 and set in post-war Perth, it won the Miles Franklin Award, one of four Winton has taken.
hook: Winton has four Miles Franklins — more than any other novelist.

question: Who painted The Starry Night?
explanation: Painted in 1889 from the window of an asylum at Saint-Rémy, it depicts a view he saw before sunrise with an imagined village added.
hook: Painted from an asylum window, with the village invented.

question: Which novel opens with the line 'Call me Ishmael'?
distractors: The Old Man and the Sea
explanation: Herman Melville's 1851 novel sold poorly in his lifetime and was only reappraised as a masterpiece in the 1920s, thirty years after his death.
hook: It flopped completely and was rediscovered three decades after Melville died.

question: Who composed the Ninth Symphony containing the Ode to Joy?
explanation: Completed in 1824 when he was almost totally deaf, it was the first major symphony to use voices; the Ode to Joy is now the anthem of the European Union.
hook: He was too deaf to hear the applause and had to be turned around to see it.

question: Which Shakespeare play features the three witches and 'Double, double toil and trouble'?
explanation: Theatrical superstition holds that saying the play's name inside a theatre brings bad luck, so actors call it 'the Scottish play'.
hook: Actors will not say the title indoors — it is 'the Scottish play'.

question: Which author wrote the dystopian novel Nineteen Eighty-Four?
explanation: Published in 1949 and written on the Scottish island of Jura while he was dying of tuberculosis; the title is often said to invert 1948, the year he finished it.
hook: He wrote it on a remote Scottish island while dying, and the title may just be 1948 reversed.

question: Which artist cut off part of his own ear in 1888?
explanation: The incident in Arles followed a violent argument with Paul Gauguin; he sold very few paintings in his lifetime and died at thirty-seven.
hook: An argument with Gauguin, and the most famous ear in art history.

question: Who wrote the Harry Potter series?
explanation: The first book was rejected by twelve publishers before Bloomsbury took it, on the advice of the chairman's eight-year-old daughter.
hook: Twelve publishers said no; a child talked the thirteenth into it.

question: Which sculpture by Michelangelo stands over five metres tall in Florence?
explanation: Carved from 1501 to 1504 from a block other sculptors had abandoned as flawed; the original now stands in the Accademia with a copy outside the Palazzo Vecchio.
hook: The marble had been rejected as unusable before he touched it.

question: Who wrote the novel To Kill a Mockingbird?
explanation: Published in 1960, it won the Pulitzer and remained her only published novel until Go Set a Watchman, an earlier draft, appeared in 2015.
hook: One novel for fifty-five years, and the second was really the first draft.

question: Which composer wrote The Four Seasons?
explanation: Published in 1725, each concerto is paired with a sonnet, possibly written by the composer himself, describing the scene the music depicts.
hook: Each concerto comes with its own poem explaining what the music is describing.

question: Which Australian building was designed by Danish architect Jørn Utzon?
explanation: His 1957 competition entry was reportedly rescued from a rejection pile; he resigned in 1966 amid political disputes and never saw the finished building.
hook: He quit before it opened and never returned to see it.

question: Who wrote The Great Gatsby?
explanation: Published in 1925 to modest sales, it was rediscovered when copies were distributed to American troops during the Second World War.
hook: It became a classic because the army handed it out to soldiers.

question: Which artist is famous for painting melting clocks in The Persistence of Memory?
explanation: Painted in 1931, the soft watches were reportedly inspired by camembert cheese melting in the sun rather than by relativity, as is often claimed.
hook: The clocks came from melting cheese, not from Einstein.

question: Who wrote the epic poem The Odyssey?
explanation: Virgil wrote the Aeneid in deliberate imitation of it; whether Homer was one person, several, or a tradition of oral performers is still debated.
hook: Homer for Greek, Virgil for Roman — the Aeneid is the sequel Rome wrote for itself.

question: Which ceiling did Michelangelo paint between 1508 and 1512?
explanation: He worked standing on scaffolding, not lying down as legend has it, and considered himself a sculptor pressed unwillingly into painting.
hook: He painted it standing up, and complained about the job the entire time.

question: Which novel features the characters Sherlock Holmes and Dr Watson?
explanation: Arthur Conan Doyle introduced them in 1887 and later killed Holmes off at the Reichenbach Falls, only to revive him after a decade of public outcry.
hook: Doyle killed Holmes and was forced by readers to bring him back.

question: Which Australian artist is best known for his series of Ned Kelly paintings?
explanation: The 1946-47 series reduced Kelly to a black helmet shape against the bush, and is held by the National Gallery of Australia.
hook: Kelly became a black rectangle with a slot — the most recognisable shape in Australian art.

question: Who wrote the Chronicles of Narnia?
explanation: He and Tolkien were close friends in the Oxford group known as the Inklings, though Tolkien disliked Narnia's mixing of mythologies.
hook: Tolkien was his best friend and thought Narnia was a mess.

question: Which instrument did Louis Armstrong famously play?
explanation: He began on cornet, moved to trumpet, and effectively invented the jazz solo as a form; his 1964 recording of Hello, Dolly! knocked the Beatles off the US number one spot.
hook: At sixty-two he knocked the Beatles off number one.

question: Who wrote the novel Frankenstein?
explanation: She was eighteen when she conceived it during a wet summer at Lake Geneva in 1816, in a ghost-story contest with Byron and her future husband.
hook: Written at eighteen, out of a rained-out holiday and a dare.

question: Which art movement is Claude Monet most associated with?
explanation: The movement took its name from a hostile review of his painting Impression, Sunrise in 1874; the artists then adopted the insult as their label.
hook: The name started as an insult from a critic, and they kept it.

question: Which poet wrote 'The Man from Snowy River'?
explanation: Published in the Bulletin in 1890, he also wrote Waltzing Matilda and Clancy of the Overflow; Lawson was his contemporary and literary sparring partner.
hook: Paterson romanticised the bush, Lawson found it grim — they argued about it in print.

question: Which novel by Charles Dickens begins 'It was the best of times, it was the worst of times'?
explanation: Published in 1859 and set during the French Revolution, it is among the best-selling novels ever written; the two cities are London and Paris.
hook: The two cities are London and Paris, and the book has sold in the hundreds of millions.

question: Which Italian artist painted The Birth of Venus?
explanation: Painted around 1485 for the Medici, it was among the first large-scale canvases in Renaissance Tuscany rather than a wooden panel or fresco.
hook: One of the first big Renaissance works painted on canvas rather than wood.

question: Who wrote the play A Streetcar Named Desire?
explanation: It won the 1948 Pulitzer and made Marlon Brando a star; the streetcar line named Desire genuinely ran in New Orleans.
hook: There really was a Desire streetcar line in New Orleans.

question: Which Australian poet wrote 'I love a sunburnt country'?
explanation: The line comes from My Country, written in 1904 when she was homesick in England at the age of nineteen.
hook: Written by a homesick teenager in England, not in the sunburnt country at all.

question: Which composer was deaf for much of his later career?
explanation: His hearing began failing in his late twenties; he continued composing by feeling vibrations through the floor and his conversation books survive as a record.
hook: He wrote his greatest works after he could no longer hear them.

question: Which novel features the character Elizabeth Bennet?
explanation: Austen called her 'as delightful a creature as ever appeared in print'; the novel's famous opening sentence about a single man in possession of a good fortune is ironic.
hook: Austen herself said she was the most delightful character in print.

question: Who painted Guernica in response to the bombing of a Basque town?
explanation: Painted in 1937 in black, white and grey, it hung in New York for decades at his insistence until Spain returned to democracy.
hook: He refused to let it go to Spain while Franco lived.

question: Which playwright wrote The Importance of Being Earnest?
explanation: It premiered in February 1895 at the height of his fame; within months he was imprisoned for gross indecency and his name was removed from the playbills.
hook: His greatest triumph and his ruin came within three months of each other.

question: Which title is Macbeth granted after the witches' first prophecy comes true?
explanation: He is already Thane of Glamis when the play opens; Macduff is Thane of Fife, and it is his family Macbeth later murders.
hook: Glamis he has, Cawdor he gets, king he takes — the three-step prophecy.

question: Which Australian became the country's only Nobel laureate in Literature, in 1973?
explanation: He won for an epic and psychological narrative art that introduced a new continent into literature, and used the prize money to fund an award for older unrecognised writers.
hook: He gave the prize money away to fund an award for overlooked writers.

question: Which novel won Richard Flanagan the 2014 Booker Prize?
answer: The Narrow Road to the Deep North
distractors: The Sound of One Hand Clapping
explanation: Set among Australian prisoners on the Burma Railway, it draws on his father's experience; the title comes from a work by the Japanese poet Bashō.
hook: The title is borrowed from Bashō — a Japanese poem for a book about Japanese captivity.

question: Which artist created the readymade sculpture Fountain, a signed urinal?
explanation: Submitted anonymously to a 1917 New York exhibition and rejected, it is now regularly voted the most influential artwork of the twentieth century; the original is lost.
hook: The most influential artwork of the century, and no original survives.

question: Which novel by Peter Carey won the Booker Prize in 2001?
answer: True History of the Kelly Gang
explanation: Written in Kelly's unpunctuated voice, it made Carey one of the few writers to win the Booker twice, having taken it for Oscar and Lucinda in 1988.
hook: Carey has two Bookers — Oscar and Lucinda in 1988, Ned Kelly in 2001.

question: Which Shakespeare play is set on an island ruled by Prospero?
explanation: Generally taken as his last solo play, Prospero's renunciation of magic is often read as Shakespeare's own farewell to the stage.
hook: Prospero drowning his book is usually read as Shakespeare retiring.

question: Which artist is famous for Campbell's Soup Cans and screenprints of Marilyn Monroe?
explanation: A leader of American Pop Art, he ran a studio called the Factory and predicted that everyone would be world-famous for fifteen minutes.
hook: The fifteen minutes of fame line is his, and he meant it as a warning.

question: Which Russian novelist wrote War and Peace?
explanation: Published serially from 1865, he insisted it was not a novel at all; it runs to well over half a million words and contains substantial passages in French.
hook: He denied it was a novel, and much of it is in French.

question: Which painting was stolen from Oslo's National Gallery in 1994 and recovered months later?
explanation: Edvard Munch made several versions; thieves left a note reading 'thanks for the poor security', and a different version was stolen again in 2004.
hook: The thieves left a thank-you note mocking the security.

question: Which Australian novelist wrote Schindler's Ark, the basis for Schindler's List?
explanation: It won the 1982 Booker Prize amid debate about whether a work drawing so heavily on documented fact qualified as a novel.
hook: A Booker won by a book people argued was not really fiction.

question: Which composer wrote the operas The Ring of the Nibelung?
explanation: The four-opera cycle takes about fifteen hours and he built a purpose-designed theatre at Bayreuth to stage it, still used for annual festivals.
hook: He built an entire theatre because no existing one could stage it properly.

question: Which novel opens 'It is a truth universally acknowledged'?
explanation: The sentence is ironic: it is the neighbourhood's assumption, not the narrator's, that a wealthy single man must want a wife.
hook: The famous line is a joke at the neighbours' expense, not a statement of fact.

question: Which Dutch painter created The Night Watch?
explanation: Completed in 1642, the painting was later trimmed to fit a wall in Amsterdam's town hall, permanently removing figures from the left side.
hook: It was cut down to fit a wall, and the missing figures are gone for good.

question: Which literary award is Australia's most prestigious for a novel of Australian life?
explanation: Funded by the estate of the author of My Brilliant Career, it requires the novel to present Australian life in any of its phases, a clause that has caused repeated controversy.
hook: The 'Australian life' clause in the will has caused arguments for seventy years.

question: Which Irish writer wrote Ulysses?
explanation: Published in 1922, it follows one day in Dublin, 16 June 1904, now celebrated as Bloomsday; the date is when he first walked out with Nora Barnacle.
hook: The whole novel happens on the day he first went walking with his future wife.

question: Which artist painted the ceiling fresco known as The Creation of Adam?
explanation: The shape surrounding God has been argued to resemble a cross-section of the human brain, though whether that was intentional remains speculation.
hook: The red cloak around God looks strikingly like a brain in cross-section.

question: Which Australian artist won the Archibald Prize and painted Alchemy?
explanation: He won the Archibald, Wynne and Sulman prizes in the same year in 1978, a feat unmatched before or since.
hook: He swept all three major prizes in a single year — nobody else has.

question: Which novel by Emily Brontë is set on the Yorkshire moors?
explanation: Her only novel, published in 1847 under the pen name Ellis Bell; Jane Eyre was by her sister Charlotte and Agnes Grey by Anne.
hook: Three sisters, three novels, three male pen names — Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell.

question: Which artist painted the Water Lilies series at his garden in Giverny?
explanation: He produced around 250 paintings of the pond over thirty years, working on with increasingly severe cataracts that visibly altered his palette.
hook: You can date the late ones by how his cataracts changed the colours.

question: Which playwright wrote Waiting for Godot?
explanation: First staged in French in 1953, he wrote it in French and translated it himself; he described it as a play in which nothing happens, twice.
hook: Famously summarised as a play where nothing happens — twice.

question: Which Colombian author wrote One Hundred Years of Solitude?
explanation: The 1967 novel defined magical realism and won him the 1982 Nobel; he reportedly sold his car to fund the writing of it.
hook: He sold the family car to buy time to finish it.

question: Which Australian Indigenous artist was famous for watercolour landscapes of the Central Desert?
explanation: He became the first Aboriginal person granted Australian citizenship, in 1957, while most Aboriginal people remained under restrictive state laws.
hook: He was given citizenship in his own country as a special exception.

question: Which Greek tragedy features a king who unknowingly kills his father and marries his mother?
explanation: Sophocles' play gave Freud the name for his theory; Antigone, also by Sophocles, concerns Oedipus's daughter.
hook: Sophocles wrote both Oedipus and the sequel about his daughter Antigone.

question: Which artist's blue and rose periods preceded his invention of Cubism?
explanation: He developed Cubism with Georges Braque from around 1907, breaking objects into simultaneous viewpoints; the two worked so closely their canvases are sometimes hard to tell apart.
hook: Blue, then rose, then Cubism — and Braque was there for the third.

question: Which novel by Margaret Atwood is set in the Republic of Gilead?
explanation: Published in 1985, she has said she included nothing that had not happened somewhere at some point in history; the sequel The Testaments won the Booker in 2019.
hook: Her rule while writing: nothing in it that had not already happened somewhere.

question: Which composer wrote the opera The Magic Flute?
explanation: Premiered in September 1791, weeks before his death at thirty-five; it is a Singspiel, with spoken dialogue rather than continuous sung recitative.
hook: Premiered weeks before he died, and it has spoken dialogue like a musical.

question: Which Australian novel by Miles Franklin was published in 1901?
distractors: For the Term of His Natural Life
explanation: Written when she was a teenager, she withdrew it from publication for decades because her family recognised themselves in it; the 1979 film starred Judy Davis.
hook: She suppressed her own book for decades because relatives took offence.

question: Which movement in art is characterised by dripped and poured paint on large canvases?
explanation: Jackson Pollock's drip technique made him its emblem; the National Gallery of Australia's purchase of Blue Poles for $1.3 million in 1973 caused a national political row.
hook: Blue Poles cost $1.3 million in 1973 and nearly became an election issue.

question: Which poet wrote 'Do not go gentle into that good night'?
explanation: Written in 1947 as his father was dying, it is a villanelle, a strict nineteen-line form with two repeating refrains.
hook: It is a villanelle — the repetition is a rule of the form, not a stylistic choice.

question: Which novel features Captain Ahab's pursuit of a white whale?
explanation: Melville drew on the real sinking of the whaleship Essex by a sperm whale in 1820, whose survivors resorted to cannibalism.
hook: Based on a real whale that sank a real ship — the Essex, in 1820.

question: Which Australian playwright wrote The Removalists and Don's Party?
explanation: He became Australia's most performed playwright from the 1970s; Ray Lawler's Summer of the Seventeenth Doll had opened the way in 1955.
hook: Lawler broke the ground in 1955; Williamson built the house in the 1970s.

question: Which French novelist wrote In Search of Lost Time?
explanation: At around 1.2 million words it is often cited as the longest novel ever published; the madeleine dipped in tea occurs early in the first volume.
hook: Longest novel ever published, and the famous cake appears in the first hundred pages.

question: Which sculptor created The Thinker?
explanation: It began as part of a larger work, The Gates of Hell, depicting Dante contemplating his poem, before being enlarged and cast independently.
hook: He is not thinking in general — he is Dante looking down into hell.

question: Which Shakespeare character says 'To be, or not to be'?
explanation: The soliloquy weighs existence against suicide and comes in Act 3, well after the play's midpoint, not at its opening as often assumed.
hook: It comes in Act 3, not at the start — a common misremembering.

question: Which Nigerian author wrote Things Fall Apart?
explanation: Published in 1958, it takes its title from Yeats's poem The Second Coming and is the most widely read African novel in English.
hook: The title is lifted straight from a Yeats poem.

question: Which architectural style is characterised by pointed arches and flying buttresses?
explanation: The name was originally a Renaissance insult implying barbarism; Romanesque used round arches and much thicker walls to carry the same loads.
hook: 'Gothic' began as an insult meaning barbaric.

question: Which author created the detective Hercule Poirot?
explanation: She is the best-selling novelist of all time, and killed Poirot off in Curtain, written during the Second World War but published in 1975.
hook: She wrote his death in the 1940s and locked it in a vault for thirty years.

question: Which Australian singer-songwriter wrote 'From Little Things Big Things Grow' with Kev Carmody?
explanation: Written in 1991, it tells the story of Vincent Lingiari and the Gurindji walk-off at Wave Hill that led to the first land handback in 1975.
hook: A song that is really a history lesson about the Wave Hill walk-off.

question: Which novel by George Orwell features the commandment 'All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others'?
explanation: Published in 1945, several publishers rejected it for offending the Soviet ally; T.S. Eliot at Faber was among those who turned it down.
hook: T.S. Eliot rejected it for being politically inconvenient in 1944.

question: Which artist painted American Gothic, showing a farmer with a pitchfork?
explanation: Painted in 1930, the models were his dentist and his sister, and the pair are meant to be father and daughter rather than husband and wife.
hook: The models were his dentist and his sister, posed as father and daughter.

question: Which Australian was the first to win the Booker Prize, in 1982?
explanation: Schindler's Ark took the prize in 1982; Peter Carey followed in 1988 and 2001, and Richard Flanagan in 2014, making four Booker wins for Australia.
hook: Keneally 1982, Carey 1988 and 2001, Flanagan 2014 — the whole Australian list.

question: Which Italian poet wrote the Divine Comedy?
explanation: Written in Tuscan vernacular rather than Latin, it helped establish modern Italian; Virgil guides him through hell and purgatory but cannot enter paradise.
hook: Virgil takes him as far as paradise and then has to stop — he was a pagan.

question: Which artist painted The Garden of Earthly Delights?
explanation: The triptych was painted around 1500 and its right panel of hell includes a figure with musical notation written on his buttocks, which musicians have since transcribed and performed.
hook: Someone transcribed the tune written on a damned soul's backside — it exists as a recording.

question: Which Australian novelist wrote The Man Who Loved Children?
explanation: Published in 1940 to little notice, it was rediscovered in 1965 after an essay by Randall Jarrell and is now widely regarded as a masterpiece.
hook: Ignored for twenty-five years until one critic's essay resurrected it.

question: Which Australian author wrote under the pen name Henry Handel Richardson?
explanation: She adopted a male name to be taken seriously; her trilogy The Fortunes of Richard Mahony traces a doctor's decline during and after the gold rushes.
hook: Another Australian woman who published under a man's name to be read.

question: Which composer wrote the Enigma Variations?
explanation: Each variation portrays a friend, and he hinted at a hidden theme running through the whole work that he never revealed; theories are still published.
hook: He took the secret theme to his grave and people are still guessing.

question: Which novel by Vladimir Nabokov is told through a fictional poem and its commentary?
explanation: Published in 1962, it presents a 999-line poem followed by an unreliable editor's notes, and can be read in almost any order.
hook: A novel disguised as a poem plus footnotes, readable in any order you like.

question: Which artist showed at the 1997 Venice Biennale after taking up painting in her late seventies?
explanation: Australia's 1997 pavilion, Fluent, showed her alongside Yvonne Koolmatrie and Judy Watson; she had produced some 3,000 works in the eight years before her death in 1996.
hook: She started painting at nearly eighty and made three thousand works in eight years.

question: Which Japanese novelist wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel?
explanation: Written around 1010 by a lady of the Heian court, it predates European novels by centuries; Sei Shōnagon was a contemporary and rival diarist.
hook: The first novel was written by a Japanese woman a thousand years ago.

question: Which painter is associated with the Heidelberg School of Australian impressionism?
explanation: Working with Arthur Streeton and Frederick McCubbin from the 1880s, he painted Shearing the Rams and The Big Picture of the opening of federal parliament.
hook: Roberts, Streeton and McCubbin — the Heidelberg trio who invented the Australian landscape look.

question: Which poet wrote the collection Leaves of Grass, revised throughout his life?
explanation: First published at his own expense in 1855 with twelve poems, it grew across nine editions to more than 400 by the 1892 'deathbed' edition.
hook: One book, nine editions, thirty-seven years of revision.

question: Which artist created the installation The Physical Impossibility of Death in the Mind of Someone Living?
explanation: The 1991 work is a tiger shark in formaldehyde; the original specimen decayed and had to be replaced, raising questions about what the artwork actually is.
hook: The shark rotted and was swapped — so is it still the same artwork?

question: Which Shakespeare play contains the stage direction 'Exit, pursued by a bear'?
explanation: It marks the abrupt tonal shift at the play's midpoint; scholars still argue over whether a real bear or a costumed actor was used at the Globe.
hook: Nobody knows whether the Globe used a costume or an actual bear.

question: Which twentieth-century composer wrote the ballet The Rite of Spring, which caused a riot at its premiere?
explanation: The 1913 Paris premiere provoked uproar over its dissonance and Nijinsky's choreography; the disturbance was probably as much about the dancing as the music.
hook: The riot was arguably about the choreography more than the notes.

question: Which Australian poet wrote the collection Selected Poems and the poem 'Bora Ring'?
explanation: She was also a leading conservationist and campaigner for Aboriginal land rights, helping found the Wildlife Preservation Society of Queensland.
hook: One of Australia's major poets was also one of its first serious environmentalists.

question: Which literary hoax fooled the Australian modernist journal Angry Penguins in 1944?
explanation: Two conservative poets invented a dead mechanic-poet and assembled nonsense verse in an afternoon; editor Max Harris published it and was later prosecuted for obscenity.
hook: The fake poet was more successful than his real inventors ever were.

question: Which German writer wrote Faust in two parts over sixty years?
explanation: He began it in his twenties and finished part two shortly before his death in 1832; the bargain with Mephistopheles gave the language the term 'Faustian'.
hook: Sixty years on one work, finished months before he died.

question: Which artist painted Las Meninas, in which the painter himself appears at the easel?
explanation: Painted in 1656, the perspective places the viewer where the king and queen stand, visible only as a reflection in a mirror at the back.
hook: You are standing where the king was — the mirror at the back proves it.

question: Which Australian novel won the inaugural Stella Prize in 2013?
explanation: Carrie Tiffany's novel took the first Stella, established to address the under-recognition of Australian women writers and named after Stella Miles Franklin.
hook: The Stella is named for Miles Franklin's actual first name.

question: Which architectural movement produced the Bauhaus school in Germany?
explanation: Founded by Walter Gropius in 1919 and closed under Nazi pressure in 1933, its emigrating staff spread its ideas to the United States and beyond.
hook: Shutting it down in 1933 exported its ideas to the rest of the world.

question: Which Russian composer wrote the ballets Swan Lake and The Nutcracker?
explanation: Swan Lake failed at its 1877 premiere and only became a staple after a posthumous 1895 revival with new choreography.
hook: Swan Lake flopped in his lifetime and became famous after he died.

question: Which poem by T.S. Eliot begins 'April is the cruellest month'?
distractors: The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock
explanation: Published in 1922, Ezra Pound cut it to roughly half its original length, an edit Eliot acknowledged by dedicating it to him as 'il miglior fabbro'.
hook: Pound cut half of it, and Eliot's dedication calls him 'the better craftsman'.

question: Which Australian film director made Picnic at Hanging Rock and Witness?
explanation: Part of the Australian New Wave of the 1970s, his 1975 film adapted Joan Lindsay's novel about schoolgirls vanishing, a story many still believe is true.
hook: The disappearance is fiction, but half the country thinks it really happened.

question: Which artist is known for large-scale wrapped buildings and landscapes?
explanation: With Jeanne-Claude he wrapped the Reichstag and Pont Neuf; their 1969 wrapping of Little Bay in Sydney was among the largest artworks ever made at the time.
hook: Their first monumental wrapping was an Australian coastline, not a European monument.

question: Which novel by Laurence Sterne includes a completely black page and a marbled page?
explanation: Published from 1759, its digressions and typographic games anticipate postmodern fiction by two centuries; the narrator is not born until volume three.
hook: The narrator does not manage to get himself born until volume three.

question: Which Australian author wrote The Secret River?
explanation: Published in 2005 and drawing on her own ancestor's settlement on the Hawkesbury, it won the Commonwealth Writers' Prize and was shortlisted for the Miles Franklin, and prompted a public argument with historians about fiction's claims on the past.
hook: It started a public argument between a novelist and historians about who owns the past.

question: Which Indigenous Australian author won the Miles Franklin for Carpentaria?
explanation: Her 2007 win followed Kim Scott's shared award for Benang in 2000; Scott won again for That Deadman Dance and Lucashenko for Too Much Lip.
hook: Scott 2000, Wright 2007, Scott again 2011, Lucashenko 2019 — the Miles Franklin roll.

question: Which Renaissance artist wrote the Lives of the Artists, effectively founding art history?
explanation: Published in 1550, it is the source of most Renaissance anecdotes and gave the period its name in Italian as the rinascita, or rebirth; the French 'Renaissance' came three centuries later via Michelet and Burckhardt.
hook: He invented art history and the word 'rebirth' — but not the word 'Renaissance'.

question: Which opera by Puccini is set in Japan and features the aria 'Un bel dì'?
explanation: It failed at its 1904 La Scala premiere and succeeded only after substantial revision; Turandot, set in China, was left unfinished at his death.
hook: Butterfly in Japan, Turandot in China — and he died before finishing the second.

question: Which Australian writer's Monkey Grip drew on her own Melbourne diaries?
explanation: Published in 1977, critics attacked it for reading like a diary, an accusation she has since said was essentially accurate and beside the point.
hook: Critics said it read like a diary; she agreed and said so what.

question: Which artist painted the Australian outback work Sofala in 1947?
explanation: His drought-stricken country towns redefined how Australians pictured the inland, replacing the sunny pastoralism of the Heidelberg painters.
hook: He replaced the golden Heidelberg landscape with drought and empty verandahs.

question: Which Australian portrait prize was the subject of a 1944 court case over whether a winning work was a caricature?
explanation: William Dobell's portrait of Joshua Smith was challenged in the NSW Supreme Court as a caricature rather than a portrait; the court upheld the award.
hook: A court had to rule on whether a painting counted as a portrait at all.

question: Which poet wrote the Australian modernist poem 'Five Bells'?
explanation: Written between 1935 and 1937 as an elegy for his friend Joe Lynch, who drowned in Sydney Harbour, and published in 1939; it later gave its name to a John Olsen mural in the Opera House.
hook: An elegy for a drowned friend that ended up painted on the Opera House wall.

question: Which Czech-born writer wrote The Metamorphosis?
explanation: He instructed his friend Max Brod to burn his unpublished manuscripts; Brod ignored him and published The Trial, The Castle and Amerika instead.
hook: Almost everything he is famous for was supposed to be burned.

question: Which style of Japanese woodblock print includes Hokusai's Great Wave?
explanation: The term means 'pictures of the floating world'; these cheap prints reached Europe as packing material and heavily influenced Van Gogh and Monet.
hook: They arrived in Europe as wrapping paper and changed Impressionism.

question: Which English novelist wrote Middlemarch under a male pen name?
explanation: Mary Ann Evans chose the name to be taken seriously and to avoid scrutiny of her relationship with a married man; Virginia Woolf called the novel one of the few written for grown-up people.
hook: Woolf called it one of the few English novels written for adults.

question: Which twentieth-century Australian sculpture and gallery bequest created the Museum of Old and New Art?
explanation: Funded by professional gambling winnings and opened in Hobart in 2011, MONA reshaped Tasmanian tourism and is built largely underground into a sandstone cliff.
hook: A museum funded by beating the bookmakers, cut into a Hobart cliff.

question: Which Greek playwright wrote the comedy Lysistrata?
explanation: In it the women of Greece withhold sex to force an end to the Peloponnesian War; Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides wrote tragedy, not comedy.
hook: The three great tragedians plus one great comedian — Aristophanes is the comedian.

question: Which Australian novelist wrote Remembering Babylon?
explanation: Published in 1993 about a European boy raised by Aboriginal people, it won the inaugural International Dublin Literary Award but lost the Miles Franklin to Rodney Hall's The Grisly Wife.
hook: It won the world's richest literary prize and still lost the Miles Franklin.

question: Which painter is credited with the first purely abstract paintings around 1910?
explanation: The claim is contested: Hilma af Klint produced abstract work from 1906 but stipulated it not be shown until decades after her death, so it was unknown until 1986.
hook: Hilma af Klint got there first but hid the work for eighty years.

question: Which novel by Herman Hesse follows a young Brahmin's search for enlightenment?
explanation: Published in 1922, it became a counterculture text in the 1960s; the protagonist is not the Buddha but a contemporary who meets him.
hook: The title character is not the Buddha — he meets the Buddha and walks on.

question: Which Australian arts institution holds Jackson Pollock's Blue Poles?
explanation: Bought in 1973 for A$1.3 million on Whitlam's personal authorisation, it caused a political storm and is now valued in the hundreds of millions.
hook: The most attacked purchase in Australian art turned out to be the best investment.

question: Which French writer wrote Madame Bovary and was prosecuted for obscenity?
explanation: The 1857 trial ended in acquittal and made the book a bestseller; he was famous for spending days searching for a single precise word.
hook: The obscenity trial was the best publicity the book could have had.

question: Which twentieth-century movement did André Breton define in a 1924 manifesto?
explanation: It grew out of Dada and drew on Freud's theories of the unconscious, aiming to release imagination through automatic writing and dream imagery.
hook: Dada came first and was nihilist; Surrealism came out of it with Freud attached.

question: Which Australian wrote the best-selling memoir A Fortunate Life?
explanation: Published in 1981 when he was eighty-seven and nine months before his death, his account of an orphaned childhood and Gallipoli sold over a million copies.
hook: Published at eighty-seven, nine months before he died, and it sold a million.

question: Which musical form did Johann Sebastian Bach perfect in The Well-Tempered Clavier?
explanation: The two books contain a prelude and fugue in every major and minor key, demonstrating a tuning system that made all twenty-four keys usable.
hook: Twenty-four keys, twice over, to prove a tuning system worked.

question: Which Australian Indigenous painting movement began at a settlement school in 1971?
explanation: Teacher Geoffrey Bardon encouraged Western Desert men to paint their designs in acrylic on board, launching the most significant art movement in modern Australia.
hook: It started with a schoolteacher handing out paint at a desert settlement.

question: Which poet wrote 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner'?
explanation: It opened Lyrical Ballads in 1798, the collection he produced with Wordsworth that is usually taken to begin English Romanticism.
hook: It is the first poem in the book that started English Romanticism.

question: Which architect designed the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao?
explanation: Opened in 1997, its titanium curves revived a declining industrial city so effectively that urban planners now speak of the 'Bilbao effect'.
hook: One building revived a whole city — planners named the phenomenon after it.

question: Which Australian composer wrote the opera Voss, based on Patrick White's novel?
explanation: Premiered in Adelaide in 1986 with a libretto by David Malouf, it brought together three major figures of Australian arts in one work.
hook: White's novel, Malouf's libretto, Meale's music — three heavyweights on one stage.

question: Which American poet published almost nothing in her lifetime despite writing nearly 1,800 poems?
explanation: Fewer than a dozen appeared in print before her death in 1886; her sister found the rest bound in hand-sewn booklets and had them published.
hook: Her sister found 1,800 poems sewn into little booklets after she died.

question: Which Italian film director made La Dolce Vita and 8½?
explanation: La Dolce Vita gave the word 'paparazzi' to the world, from the surname of a photographer character in the film.
hook: 'Paparazzi' is just a character's surname from one of his films.

question: Which Australian novel by Christos Tsiolkas turns on a man striking someone else's child?
explanation: Published in 2008, it tells the same incident from eight characters' perspectives and was adapted into television series in both Australia and the United States.
hook: One incident, eight narrators, two countries' television adaptations.

question: Which Spanish architect designed the still-unfinished Sagrada Família?
explanation: Begun in 1882 and taken over by him in 1883, he devoted the last years of his life to it and is buried in its crypt; completion is projected for the 2030s.
hook: Under construction for over 140 years, and the architect is buried inside it.

question: Which literary prize did Bob Dylan win in 2016, to widespread surprise?
explanation: The citation praised new poetic expressions within the great American song tradition; he did not respond for two weeks and skipped the ceremony.
hook: He ignored the Swedish Academy's calls for a fortnight, then skipped the ceremony.
